chapter_title: The Spectrum of Testing: Unit, Integration, and Acceptance
chapter_summary:
Welcome to a crucial module where we expand our TDD horizons beyond the confines of individual units. While unit tests are the bedrock of TDD, ensuring the correctness of small, isolated pieces of code, real-world applications are complex systems where these units interact. This is where integration and acceptance tests become indispensable. Understanding the spectrum of testing is vital for building robust software, and it's often visualized through the "testing pyramid." At the base of this pyramid are unit tests: fast, numerous, and focused on individual components. As we move up, we encounter integration tests, which verify the interactions between these components. At the very top, fewer in number but broader in scope, are acceptance tests, which validate the entire system against business requirements.

Let's break down these categories. **Unit tests**, as we've extensively covered, are about testing the smallest testable parts of an application in isolation. Their goal is to verify that a single function, method, or class behaves as expected. They are incredibly fast, allowing for rapid feedback, and when they fail, they pinpoint the exact location of the bug. The challenge with unit tests is that they don't tell you if your isolated components work correctly *together*. You might have two perfectly unit-tested modules, but if they don't communicate correctly, your application will still fail. This is a common mistake: assuming extensive unit test coverage guarantees a working system. It doesn't.

This is where **integration tests** step in. An integration test verifies the interactions between two or more units or components. For example, it might test if your `UserService` correctly interacts with your `UserRepository` to save a user to a database, or if your API endpoint correctly calls a service layer. Integration tests are designed to expose faults in the interfaces and interactions between integrated units. They are typically slower than unit tests because they involve more moving parts, potentially including databases, file systems, or network calls. While still automated, they require a more complex setup and teardown to ensure a clean state for each test run. The key here is to test the *seams* where components meet, ensuring data flows correctly and contracts are honored. A common pitfall is making integration tests too broad, essentially turning them into slow, brittle end-to-end tests. We want to focus on specific integration points.

Finally, at the pinnacle of the pyramid, we have **acceptance tests**, also known as end-to-end (E2E) tests or system tests. These tests validate the entire system from an end-user perspective, ensuring that the software meets the specified business requirements and user stories. An acceptance test might simulate a user logging in, navigating through a feature, and performing an action, then verifying the expected outcome. These tests are the slowest, most complex, and most expensive to maintain, as they involve the entire application stack, including the UI, backend services, and databases. They are also the most realistic, as they mimic actual user behavior. Because of their cost, we aim for fewer acceptance tests, focusing on critical user journeys and business-critical functionality. The value of acceptance tests lies in providing confidence that the complete system delivers value to the user. A common mistake is having too many acceptance tests, which slows down the feedback loop and makes the test suite brittle.

The "testing pyramid" isn't a rigid rule but a guiding heuristic: aim for many unit tests, a moderate number of integration tests, and a small number of acceptance tests. This balance optimizes for fast feedback, comprehensive coverage, and confidence in the overall system. TDD, while often associated with unit testing, encourages us to think about tests at all levels. We start with a failing acceptance test (often expressed as a user story), then break it down into smaller integration tests, and finally, drive the implementation with unit tests. This outside-in approach, sometimes called "double-loop TDD" or "outside-in TDD," ensures that every piece of code serves a higher-level purpose, ultimately contributing to a feature that satisfies a user requirement. By understanding and applying these different testing levels, we build a robust safety net around our software, catching bugs early and ensuring that our applications are not only correct but also deliver real value.

screens.title: The Spectrum of Testing
screens.subtitle: Unit, Integration, and Acceptance tests in TDD

narration.text: In this lesson we expand your view of testing beyond single functions. You'll learn a practical spectrum that places unit tests at the base, integration tests in the middle, and acceptance or end-to-end tests at the top. Each level answers a different question: does this small piece behave correctly, do components interact correctly, and does the whole system deliver value to a user? We’ll use the testing pyramid as a guiding heuristic to balance speed, confidence, and realism. You will also see how Test-Driven Development is not just about isolated unit tests but can be practiced outside-in, starting from a failing acceptance test and moving inward to integration and unit tests. Throughout the lesson we will use short e-commerce examples to ground abstract ideas, highlight common mistakes like over-relying on unit tests or having too many brittle acceptance tests, and end with an activity that asks you to classify scenarios. By the end you will know when to write a fast isolated test, when to test an integration seam, and how to decide which user journeys deserve acceptance coverage. Ready to map tests to purpose and cost?

keyIdea.title: Testing is layered
keyIdea.text: Different test levels trade speed and isolation for realism. Use many unit tests, moderate integration tests, and a few acceptance tests.

screens.title: Unit Tests: Purpose and Characteristics
screens.subtitle: Why unit tests are the bedrock of TDD

narration.text: Unit tests verify the smallest testable parts of your application: a function, method, or class. Their purpose is to provide very fast feedback and precise failure localization. In practice this means you write many small tests that mock or stub dependencies so the test focuses only on the unit's behavior. A concrete example is testing a product price calculation function: supply known inputs and assert the returned price matches the expected amount. The advantage is speed and clarity — when a unit test fails you know where to look. A common misconception is believing that exhaustive unit testing alone guarantees a working system. Two units can behave correctly on their own but still fail to work together because of interface mismatches or data format assumptions. Another pitfall is coupling tests to implementation details rather than public behavior, which makes refactoring painful. To avoid that, test the unit's observable behavior and keep interactions mocked at explicit seams. Key takeaway: use unit tests for rapid design feedback and refactoring safety. A good check is asking whether the test pinpoints a single responsibility; if it does, it’s likely a proper unit test. How will you apply this when designing your next function?

keyIdea.title: Unit tests = fast and focused
keyIdea.text: Use unit tests for single responsibilities, quick feedback, and safe refactoring.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Unit Tests
Definition

Unit tests test the smallest parts

They isolate a single responsibility, use mocks for dependencies, and return very fast feedback suitable for TDD red-green-refactor cycles.

Concrete example
Test a price calculation method with fixed inputs and assert the exact output. Mock external tax or repository calls so only calculation logic is covered.
Key Takeaway

Unit tests are fast design guards. Favor behavioral assertions over implementation details to keep tests resilient to refactoring.

Common mistake

Relying only on unit tests and assuming the system will integrate correctly. Unit tests don't exercise real interactions or configuration nuances.

Pro tip
Keep mocks explicit and small. Name mocked behaviors to document the expected contract between the unit and its dependencies.
Example code snippet
def test_calculate_price_applies_discount():
    # Given
    item = Item(price=100)
    # When
    result = calculate_price(item, discount=0.1)
    # Then
    assert result == 90

screens.title: Unit Tests vs Integration Tests
screens.subtitle: How scope, speed, and setup differ

narration.text: Comparing unit and integration tests helps you choose where to invest effort. Unit tests run against isolated code and use mocks for external dependencies. They are extremely fast and ideal for TDD cycles, but they do not reveal interface mismatches. Integration tests exercise interactions between two or more components. For example, testing ProductService together with ProductRepository verifies that service methods call the repository correctly and that data shapes flow through. Integration tests are slower because they may touch databases or file systems and require setup and teardown to keep state consistent. A useful mental model: ask whether you are testing an implementation detail or a contract between modules. If you are testing a contract, prefer an integration test. A common mistake is making integration tests too broad, effectively turning them into slow acceptance tests that are expensive to debug. To avoid that, scope integration tests to specific seams — for example, service-to-repository calls — and keep their assertions focused on interaction outcomes rather than full UI behavior. Which seams in your application need integration coverage? Unit Tests vs Integration Tests means use unit tests for local correctness and integration tests to verify contracts between components.. In practical terms, how scope, speed, and setup differ. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Scope vs realism
keyIdea.text: Use unit tests for local correctness and integration tests to verify contracts between components.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Unit vs Integration
Unit Tests

Isolated, fast, narrow

  • Mocks dependencies to test a single behavior.
  • Provide tight feedback loops for design and refactor.
  • Failures point to a specific unit.
Example
Test a validator function's return values for various inputs without touching storage.
Integration Tests

Interactions and seams

  • Verify that components collaborate as expected.
  • Expose contract and data-flow issues between modules.
  • Require environment setup and teardown.
Scoped example
Test ProductService calling ProductRepository to ensure saved data has expected shape.
When to choose unit
When you need rapid design feedback and precise failure localization.
When to choose integration
When verifying a contract or interface between modules is the priority.
Pitfall to avoid
Making integration tests too broad and slow by including UI or unrelated services.

screens.title: Integration Tests: Seams and Setup
screens.subtitle: Testing interactions without full system overhead

narration.text: Integration tests validate that components communicate correctly across defined seams. They sit between unit and acceptance tests and are ideal for catching interface mismatches and contract violations. For example, an integration test might exercise ProductService and ProductRepository together to confirm that saving a product results in the expected database record. Because integration tests often touch external resources, they require a deterministic setup and teardown strategy so tests don't influence each other. This might involve test doubles for slow services, ephemeral databases, or in-memory substitutes. A common misconception is that integration tests must always hit a real database; in practice you can use lightweight substitutes that exercise the same code paths while keeping runs reasonably fast and repeatable. Another trap is over-scoping: writing integration tests that attempt to validate entire user journeys rather than specific interactions. Keep assertions focused on the contract you care about, and isolate unrelated subsystems with controlled doubles. Key takeaway: integration tests give higher confidence in module collaboration, but scope and environment control make them maintainable and faster than full acceptance tests. Which seams in your codebase would benefit from focused integration checks?

keyIdea.title: Exercise the seam
keyIdea.text: Integration tests prove that modules talk correctly; keep them focused and environment-controlled.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Integration Tests
What they verify

Contracts and data flow between components

Integration tests check that components exchange expected data and honor call contracts. They reveal mismatches in serialization, parameter ordering, or error handling between modules.

Scoped example: ProductService + ProductRepository produce persisted record with correct fields.
Setup tip: use ephemeral or in-memory stores to keep tests repeatable and fast.
Integration tests require careful state setup and teardown. Use fixtures or lightweight test doubles where appropriate to avoid flakiness from external services.
Common pitfalls
  • Testing too much at once and creating slow, brittle tests.
  • Assuming integration equals acceptance; they serve different purposes.
  • Not isolating unrelated systems, which increases maintenance cost.
Check your test
If your test fails, can you locate which component's contract broke? If yes, scope is appropriate.

screens.title: Acceptance Tests: Realism and Cost
screens.subtitle: Validating user journeys and business value

narration.text: Acceptance tests, also called end-to-end or system tests, validate the application from the user's perspective. They are valuable because they confirm that the entire stack delivers the expected business outcome, such as a successful purchase flow or a login sequence. A concrete example is simulating a user who adds an item to the cart, completes checkout, and then verifies the order appears in their order history. Acceptance tests are the slowest and most complex to maintain because they exercise the UI, backend services, and data stores together. They also tend to be the most realistic. Because of their cost, aim for a small set of high-value acceptance tests that cover critical user journeys rather than an exhaustive acceptance suite. A mistake many teams make is trying to replace integration tests with acceptance tests or writing too many end-to-end tests, which slows development and increases flakiness. Instead, pick acceptance checks that provide true business confidence and use integration and unit tests to cover the implementation details. Key takeaway: acceptance tests give the final assurance that your software delivers value to users, but use them sparingly and strategically. Which user journeys are most critical in your product?

keyIdea.title: Top-level assurance
keyIdea.text: Acceptance tests validate user outcomes; reserve them for critical journeys due to cost and maintenance.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Acceptance Tests
Definition

End-to-end checks for business outcomes

Acceptance tests simulate user behavior across the full stack to ensure features deliver the desired value.

Real example: Add to cart, checkout, confirm order in history.
Cost note: slow, requires cross-stack orchestration and careful environment management.
Strategy: limit to critical user journeys to keep suite maintainable.
Pitfall

Over-reliance on acceptance tests can slow feedback and yield brittle tests that break for unrelated UI changes. Use them where they uniquely provide business confidence.

screens.title: The Testing Pyramid Explained
screens.subtitle: Why the shape matters for a balanced suite

narration.text: The testing pyramid is a heuristic that helps you allocate testing effort. At the base are many unit tests that are fast and isolate small behaviors. In the middle, a moderate number of integration tests verify component contracts. At the top sit a few acceptance tests that check full user journeys. This shape optimizes for fast feedback and confidence: fast unit tests provide a quick developer loop; integration tests ensure modules work together; acceptance tests confirm the product delivers value. The pyramid is not a rigid rule — it's guidance. For some features you may invert parts of the pyramid when user-critical flows need more end-to-end confidence, but be mindful of cost. Concrete e-commerce example: one acceptance test for checkout may correspond to several integration tests for cart-to-order flows and many unit tests for pricing and validation logic. A misconception to watch for is treating the pyramid as if it prescribes exact counts instead of reflecting trade-offs. Use it to decide where bugs are most dangerous and where quick feedback matters most. How would you shape the pyramid for a high-traffic checkout feature?

keyIdea.title: Heuristic, not law
keyIdea.text: The pyramid guides coverage: prioritize fast unit tests, moderate integration coverage, and focused acceptance checks.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Testing Pyramid

Testing Pyramid

A visual heuristic that encourages a wide base of unit tests, a middle layer of integration tests, and a narrow top of acceptance tests to optimize speed and confidence.

Base: Many unit tests for fast feedback and design safety.
Middle: Integration tests for seams and contracts.
Top: Few acceptance tests for critical user journeys.
E-commerce example
One acceptance test for checkout, several integration tests for cart-to-order and payment interactions, many unit tests for price, tax, and validation logic.
Misconception

The pyramid is not a quota. Adjust counts based on risk, user value, and feedback speed.

screens.title: Outside-in TDD (Double-Loop)
screens.subtitle: Drive features from acceptance down to units

narration.text: Outside-in TDD, sometimes called double-loop TDD, begins with a failing acceptance test that represents a user story. From that high-level failing test you break the requirement into smaller integration tests focused on key seams. Each seam is then implemented and driven by unit tests that ensure the small pieces behave correctly. This approach keeps the work aligned to user value: every unit you implement is linked to an acceptance-level need. A concrete walk-through: write an acceptance test for a simple login flow that fails; identify that authentication depends on a service-to-repository seam; write an integration test for that seam; then write unit tests for the service methods and repository helpers. A common contrast is starting inside-out with unit tests only; that can produce code that is well-tested but not necessarily aligned to user needs. Outside-in helps avoid this by ensuring the top-level behavior leads design choices. Practical tip: keep acceptance tests focused on value, integration tests narrow to contracts, and unit tests precise on behavior. End with a reflective question: which user story in your backlog would benefit from an outside-in drive?

keyIdea.title: Start from value
keyIdea.text: Write a failing acceptance test first, then decompose into integration and unit tests to implement the feature.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Outside-in TDD
Workflow

Acceptance → Integration → Unit

  1. Write a failing acceptance test for the user story.
  2. Break it into integration tests for important seams.
  3. Drive implementation with focused unit tests for each component.
This double-loop keeps development tied to user value and ensures each unit serves a higher-level purpose.
Concrete example
Start with a failing checkout acceptance test, add integration tests for payment and order creation seams, then write unit tests for price calculation and order validation functions.
Key Takeaway

Outside-in TDD aligns code to user needs and reduces the risk of well-tested but irrelevant implementations.

screens.title: Trade-offs: Isolation, Speed, Realism
screens.subtitle: Choosing the right test for the job

narration.text: Every test level trades off isolation, execution speed, and realism. Unit tests maximize isolation and speed but give the least realism. Integration tests increase realism by exercising component interactions, at the cost of slower runs and added environment work. Acceptance tests maximize realism by exercising the whole stack, but they are slowest and most expensive to maintain. When choosing test coverage, consider the risk of a bug slipping to production, the cost of diagnosing failures, and how quickly you need feedback during development. For example, a pricing function that affects billing should have strong unit coverage because computation errors are costly and easily isolated. A cross-service orchestration that is sensitive to message formats benefits from integration tests. Critical end-to-end business flows like checkout deserve focused acceptance tests. Misconception: thinking tests are free; they require time to write, maintain, and run. Use this cost model to decide which tests are worth investing in. A practical rule: drive high-risk, high-value features with acceptance tests and cover implementation details with faster tests. What trade-off will you prioritize for your next release? Trade-offs: Isolation, Speed, Realism means match test level to the risk and value of the behavior being protected.. In practical terms, choosing the right test for the job. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Weigh cost vs value
keyIdea.text: Match test level to the risk and value of the behavior being protected.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Trade-offs

Isolation, Speed, Realism

Consider what you are willing to trade: fast feedback or realistic coverage. Different features need different balances.
Unit: high isolation, very fast, low realism.
Integration: medium realism, medium speed, tests contracts.
Acceptance: high realism, slow, high maintenance cost.
Decision heuristics
  • Protect critical business flows with acceptance tests.
  • Protect seams and integrations with focused integration tests.
  • Protect algorithmic and local logic with unit tests.
Practical rule

Use the pyramid to guide allocation, but adjust based on risk and feedback needs.

screens.title: Classifying Tests: E-commerce Examples
screens.subtitle: Map unit, integration, and acceptance scenarios to code

narration.text: Let's ground the ideas with the provided e-commerce example. The ProductService uses a ProductRepository to fetch and save products. A unit test for ProductService. get_product_details would mock ProductRepository. find_by_id to return a known product and assert the returned dictionary structure. This verifies logic inside ProductService in isolation. An integration test would instantiate ProductRepository (or a test double that closely simulates the database) and run ProductService. get_product_details to ensure the service and repository interoperate correctly and return consistent data; this catches mismatches in data shape or interaction. An acceptance test for the /products/ endpoint would exercise the full stack: start the web layer, call the endpoint, and verify the HTTP response and payload, confirming the system delivers what users expect. A common misconception is confusing integration tests with acceptance tests; remember integration focuses on component contracts while acceptance verifies end-user outcomes. Practice classifying scenarios by asking: what failure would this test catch, how long will it take to run, and can the failure be pinned to a single component? This checklist helps you choose the right level for each scenario. Classifying Tests: E-commerce Examples means choose test level based on what failure you want to detect and how quickly you need feedback.. In practical terms, map unit, integration, and acceptance scenarios to code. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Classify by failure mode
keyIdea.text: Choose test level based on what failure you want to detect and how quickly you need feedback.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Classifying Tests
Unit test scenario
Mock ProductRepository.find_by_id to return a product object and assert ProductService.get_product_details returns the expected dictionary.
# Unit test pseudocode
mock_repo.find_by_id.return_value = Product(id=1, name='Laptop', price=1200)
result = product_service.get_product_details(1)
assert result == {'id':1,'name':'Laptop','price':1200}
Integration test scenario
Use a test double or ephemeral store for ProductRepository and call ProductService.get_product_details to ensure the service and repository exchange correct shapes and data.
Goal: catch interface mismatches and serialization issues between service and repository.
Acceptance test scenario
Start the web layer, call GET /products/1, and assert the HTTP response body matches the expected product JSON and status codes. This checks the whole stack including routing and serialization.
Checklist

For each scenario ask: what failure will this detect, how long will it take to run, and can the cause be localized to a component?

narration.text: Now practice classifying test scenarios using the pattern we just covered. For each scenario ask: what does the test need to prove, where will the failure surface, and how long will it take to run? Scenario one: verifying that ProductService. get_product_details returns a correctly shaped dictionary when the repository returns a matching product. This is a unit test because the repository can be mocked and the assertion checks local behavior. Scenario two: testing ProductService together with ProductRepository to ensure saved data persists correctly is an integration test because it checks the seam between service and storage. Scenario three: calling the /products/ endpoint and verifying the HTTP response is an acceptance test because it exercises routing, serialization, and business logic end-to-end. A common mistake is describing scenario two as acceptance; instead keep integration tests focused on the service-to-repo seam and avoid bringing in UI elements. Practice by writing short descriptions for each scenario—what to mock, what to assert, and why that level fits. That habit quickly improves how you distribute tests across the pyramid. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Classify Scenarios
Scenario 1
Unit test for ProductService.get_product_details with mocked repository to assert returned dictionary shape.
What to mock: repository.find_by_id. What to assert: returned id, name, price. Why: isolates service logic for fast feedback.
Scenario 2
Integration test that uses a test double or ephemeral DB to verify ProductService saves and retrieves products correctly.
What to setup: ephemeral repository. What to assert: persisted fields and return structure. Why: verifies service and repository seam.
Scenario 3
Acceptance test calling GET /products/, verifying HTTP status and response body across the full stack.
What to run: full app stack. What to assert: HTTP status and JSON payload. Why: ensures end-to-end behavior meets user expectations.
Reflection prompt

For each scenario practice writing a one-paragraph test description: what to mock, what to assert, and why the level matches.

screens.title: Avoiding Fragile and Slow Test Suites
screens.subtitle: Patterns that lead to brittleness or slowness

narration.text: Teams often create fragile test suites by making tests depend on unrelated subsystems or by asserting implementation details. One common mistake is mocking too little, which turns unit-level checks into slow integration-style runs that are hard to maintain. The inverse mistake is mocking too much and asserting internal calls, which couples tests to implementation and makes refactoring expensive. Another frequent issue is over-using acceptance tests for coverage; this slows the feedback loop and produces brittle tests that break for minor UI changes. To prevent these problems, scope tests to a clear purpose: unit tests should assert observable behavior, integration tests should verify contracts, and acceptance tests should validate key user journeys only. Use the practical checklist: can the test be executed quickly, does it single out a probable cause on failure, and does the test align with a risk or business value? If the answer is no, reconsider the test’s level and assertions. Key takeaway: keep tests purposeful and maintainable by aligning their scope to the failure you want to catch. What brittle test will you simplify first? Avoiding Fragile and Slow Test Suites means avoid coupling to internals and avoid bloating acceptance coverage; scope tests by the failure you need to catch.. In practical terms, patterns that lead to brittleness or slowness. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Make tests purposeful
keyIdea.text: Avoid coupling to internals and avoid bloating acceptance coverage; scope tests by the failure you need to catch.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Common Mistakes

Brittleness causes

  • Asserting internal calls instead of public behavior.
  • Entangling unit tests with external services.
  • Having too many broad acceptance tests for coverage.

Remedies

Redesign tests to target a single failure mode, use doubles where appropriate, and reserve acceptance tests for flows that require whole-stack validation.
Checklist: fast execution, clear fault localization, alignment with business risk.
Warning

A growing, slow test suite reduces developer velocity. Periodically prune or refactor brittle tests and reassign coverage to faster levels when possible.

screens.title: Balancing Your Test Suite Over Time
screens.subtitle: Practical steps to maintain a healthy pyramid

narration.text: Maintaining a balanced test suite is an ongoing activity. Begin with a small acceptance test for the highest-value user story, then write integration tests for the key seams exposed by that story, and fill in unit tests to support implementation. Over time, monitor test run times and failure rates to identify slow or flaky tests that harm feedback loops. When a test is flaky or slow, decide whether it should be rewritten at a lower level, isolated with better fixtures, or removed if it duplicates faster checks. Schedule periodic reviews to prune redundant acceptance tests and to convert brittle end-to-end checks into focused integration tests when appropriate. Another practical habit is to prioritize fixing failing tests during the same sprint rather than accumulating technical debt. This keeps the pyramid healthy and the suite valuable. Finally, learn to communicate test strategy as trade-offs to product stakeholders so coverage maps to business risk. Which maintenance habit will you adopt first to keep your suite effective? keyIdea.text: Regularly prune, refactor, and reassign tests to keep feedback fast and confidence high.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Balancing Tests

Practical maintenance timeline

  1. Start: a small acceptance test for a high-value user story.
  2. Next: add integration tests for essential seams.
  3. Then: fill in unit tests to drive implementation and refactoring safety.
  4. Ongoing: monitor run-times, fix flakiness, prune redundant acceptance tests.
Quick rules
  • Fix failing tests quickly.
  • Prefer focused integration checks over broad end-to-end ones.
  • Prune or rework slow tests.
Key Takeaway

A healthy suite is actively curated. Trade maintenance cost against the business value each test provides.

narration.text: Let's recap the most important concepts to remember. First, unit tests verify the smallest parts of code in isolation; they are fast and help with design and refactoring. Second, integration tests verify interactions between components and expose interface or contract issues that unit tests cannot. Third, acceptance tests validate end-to-end user journeys and confirm the system delivers business value. Each test level serves a clear purpose and has different costs and benefits. Use the testing pyramid as a practical heuristic: many unit tests at the base, a moderate number of integration tests in the middle, and a small number of high-value acceptance tests at the top. Avoid common pitfalls such as over-relying on a single test level or making tests brittle by asserting internals. Finally, practice outside-in TDD when you need to align implementation to a user story: write a failing acceptance test, break it into integrations, and drive units with focused tests. Carry these concepts forward as rules of thumb to guide your test strategy.

keyIdea.title: Remember the pyramid
keyIdea.text: Many unit tests, some integration tests, few acceptance tests — align tests to risk and value.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Key Concepts
Unit Test
Verifies a single small unit in isolation. Fast, numerous, and precise when diagnosing failures.
Integration Test
Checks interactions between components and uncovers interface and data-flow issues.
Acceptance Test
Validates whole user journeys and business requirements. Use sparingly for critical flows.
Summary takeaway: distribute tests by risk and feedback needs. Prefer many fast unit tests, moderate integration coverage for seams, and a focused set of acceptance tests for value-critical journeys.

narration.text: A few final concise reminders. Testing pyramid: a heuristic recommending many unit tests, fewer integration tests, and even fewer acceptance tests to balance feedback speed and confidence. Outside-in TDD: start with a failing acceptance test and decompose into integration and unit tests so every implemented unit ties to user value. Use these two ideas together: let the pyramid guide coverage and use outside-in TDD to ensure tests are purposeful and aligned to features. Regularly review your suite to remove brittle or redundant tests and to move checks to faster levels when appropriate.
